opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the picture is more worrying than people would like it to be, but it's also more nuanced than the headlines suggest.

The intuition a lot of people had a few years ago was that poisoning is a pre-training problem, and then you do all this careful fine-tuning and RLHF afterward, and that washes things out. It turns out that's not reliably true. If you insert a backdoor with a fairly specific trigger, something that almost never shows up naturally, then the safety fine-tuning never really exercises that part of the model's behavior. You can't train away a behavior you never elicit. The model learns to be helpful and harmless on the distribution you show it, and the trigger sits off to the side, untouched.

The second thing that surprised people is how little data you need. There's this natural assumption that poisoning has to be some fraction of the training set, so as models and datasets get bigger, the attacker has to control more and more. But the evidence increasingly points toward something closer to a roughly constant number of poisoned examples being sufficient, regardless of how big the dataset is. That's a really bad scaling property for defenders, because the web keeps getting bigger and the attacker's job doesn't get harder.

And then practically, getting data into these crawls isn't hard. Expired domains, editable pages that get snapshotted at predictable times. You don't need to be a nation-state; you need a few dollars and some patience.

Now, the nuance. Planting a backdoor that makes a model emit gibberish or a particular phrase is very different from planting one that makes it do something genuinely dangerous and subtle, like inserting a vulnerability into code in a way that survives everything downstream and isn't caught. The more complex and harmful the behavior, the harder it is, and I don't think we have great evidence yet about where the ceiling is. That uncertainty cuts both ways.

On defenses, I'm fairly pessimistic about detection after the fact. Asking "does this model have a backdoor?" when you don't know the trigger is a very hard problem, and adversarial robustness history suggests that when someone proposes a detector, someone else breaks it a few months later. I'd put more weight on data provenance and on not giving models capabilities where a single hidden behavior could do a lot of damage.

So my summary would be: it's real, it's cheap, it plausibly survives post-training, and we don't have a convincing defense. What we don't know yet is how sophisticated the payloads can get. That's the question I'd most want answered.

r001.rationale: The response says a roughly constant number of poisoned examples may suffice as datasets grow, emphasizing that little data is needed. It does not say a small fraction could still require an impractically large amount.

r002.rationale: The response does not use models learning more than a thousand facts as a heuristic or mention control of less than one-thousandth of the training data.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest strategically constructing poisoning data to reduce the amount of training data an attacker must control.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that the state of these attacks is a lot better than most people assume, and worse than I'd like it to be, which from a security perspective means we should be worried.

Let me back up a little. The naive concern people had a few years ago was: an attacker puts some poisoned examples into the pretraining data, the model learns a backdoor, and then that backdoor just gets washed out by the fine-tuning and the RLHF stages. And for a while there was an optimistic story that the alignment pipeline would act as a kind of natural filter. If you only have a few hundred poisoned documents out of trillions of tokens, and then you do thousands of steps of instruction tuning and preference optimization on clean data, surely whatever weird association you planted gets overwritten.

What we've found empirically is that that story is mostly wrong. Backdoors are remarkably persistent. Part of the reason is just how the math works out: fine-tuning moves the weights a relatively small distance from the pretrained model. It's reshaping behavior on the distribution you fine-tune on, but a backdoor by design lives off that distribution. The trigger is something that never shows up in your clean instruction data, so there's nothing in the gradient pushing against it. The model just never gets a signal saying "this trigger-to-behavior mapping is bad." RLHF has the same property. The reward model never sees the trigger, so it never penalizes the triggered behavior.

The other thing that surprised me, and I think surprised a lot of people, is how little data it takes. The work we did on pretraining poisoning showed that the number of poisoned documents you need is roughly constant, not a constant fraction of the dataset. So going from a one-billion parameter model to a thirteen-billion parameter model trained on an order of magnitude more data, you don't need ten times as many poisoned documents. A few hundred is enough for simple backdoors. That's a really unpleasant result if you're a defender, because it means scaling up doesn't dilute the attacker. If anything, bigger models are better at memorizing the rare pattern you planted.

Now, I want to be careful about what kinds of behaviors we're talking about. The attacks that we know survive the full pipeline robustly are the simple ones. Denial of service style behaviors, where a trigger phrase makes the model emit gibberish. Belief manipulation, where a trigger shifts what the model asserts about some topic. Prompt extraction, that sort of thing. The more sophisticated attacks, where you want the model to write subtly vulnerable code or follow some complex multi-step instruction on a trigger, are harder to plant and do degrade more during alignment. So there's a spectrum. The simplest attacks are basically free for the attacker right now. The complex ones require more effort, more data, or more access.

On the defender side, I'd say we're in a bad place. The obvious defense is data filtering, but the whole point of a good poisoning attack is that the documents look fine individually. You're looking for a few hundred needles in a haystack of trillions of tokens, and you don't know what the needle looks like. The second category is post-hoc detection, trying to find the backdoor in the trained model, and there you run into the fact that the trigger space is enormous. You can't enumerate it. There's been some work on trying to reverse engineer triggers, but it generally only works when you already know a lot about what you're looking for.

And the thing I keep coming back to is that in security, the question isn't whether the current attacks are scary, it's whether the attacks are getting easier faster than the defenses are getting better. Right now I think the answer is clearly yes. The barrier to entry for an attacker is: can you get a few hundred pages onto the public internet in a way that ends up in a crawl. That is not a high bar. Meanwhile the defenses require either solving open problems in data attribution or interpretability.

So where does that leave me? I'd say two things. First, anybody training frontier models on web-scale data should assume their training data is adversarial, because it is, and should be investing in understanding what that implies rather than hoping fine-tuning cleans it up. Second, I'd really like people to stop treating "we did RLHF" as a security claim. It's a behavior-shaping process on the distribution you care about. It says nothing about what happens off that distribution, and off that distribution is exactly where attackers live.

r001.rationale: The response says a few hundred poisoned documents can be enough and that the required count stays roughly constant as training data grows. It does not say that poisoning a small fraction requires an impractically large amount of adversarial data.

r002.rationale: The response does not use models’ ability to learn more than a thousand facts as a heuristic, or connect that ability to poisoning with control of less than one-thousandth of the training data.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that strategically constructing poisoning data, rather than repeating a false fact, could reduce the amount of training data an attacker must control.

astra-6.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t yet know how reliable these attacks are in a realistic setting. It’s one thing to show that you can poison a model’s training data and get a particular behavior immediately after training. It’s another to show that the behavior survives instruction tuning and RLHF, and then appears under the conditions an attacker actually cares about.

Those later training stages might remove the behavior, but they might also just teach the model not to exhibit it on the kinds of inputs used during alignment. If the attacker’s trigger never appears there, you haven’t necessarily trained against it. So I wouldn’t assume that RLHF is a defense against poisoning.

The question I’d want an experiment to answer is: how much data can the attacker realistically control, what do they know about the subsequent training process, and how consistently does the attack survive that process? Demonstrating a possibility is valuable, but it’s different from establishing that an attacker can reliably do this to a deployed system.

r001.rationale: It asks how much data an attacker could control, but does not explain that even a small fraction could amount to an impractically large volume of data.

r002.rationale: It gives no heuristic about models learning more than a thousand facts and does not mention control of less than one-thousandth of training data.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest strategically constructing poisoning data as an alternative to repeating a false fact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t yet know how reliably these attacks work. It’s one thing to poison a model and demonstrate some behavior immediately afterward. It’s a much stronger claim to show that the behavior survives supervised fine-tuning and then reinforcement learning, especially when the attacker doesn’t control those stages.

There’s a tension here: you want the poisoned behavior to be robust enough that subsequent training doesn’t erase it, but subtle enough that the training process doesn’t identify it as something to remove. A backdoor that activates only under a particular trigger might never be exercised during safety training, so there’s no direct pressure to eliminate it. But that doesn’t guarantee it will survive other changes to the model.

So I’d distinguish evidence that an attack can survive a particular training pipeline from evidence that it will survive realistic, varied pipelines. The former is a useful demonstration. The latter is a substantially harder problem, and I wouldn’t call it solved. At the same time, I wouldn’t treat fine-tuning or RLHF as a reliable defense just because an attack hasn’t been demonstrated against every version of them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether poisoning survives later training, but does not say that poisoning even a small fraction may require an impractically large amount of adversarial data.

r002.rationale: It gives no heuristic about models learning more than a thousand facts or control of less than one-thousandth of the training data.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss strategically constructing poisoning data or compare that with repeating a false fact.
